title: Release-process repairs found by running a release: a checksum manifest that no longer describes bytes nobody can download, a playground deploy that runs the fix it ships, and open issues that must be fixed or explained before a tag

items: Release integrity: signing rewrites the Windows installers, so the SHA256SUMS published beside them described bytes that no longer existed and verification failed on both MSIs -- the two files whose integrity matters most. The signing script re-uploaded the signed installers and never touched the manifest; the repair lived in a separate script and in whoever remembered to run it. It is now part of signing, rebuilt from the published assets and verified by re-downloading it

Playground deploys: update.sh pulls the repository from inside itself, so a run that pulled a new update.sh kept executing the old one and exited 0. A deploy reported success, moved the version it displays, and left the engine on the previous release. It now re-execs when the pull changes it, and the health check polls instead of sleeping three seconds and asking once, which had it reporting failure after every healthy restart

Release gating: a step declared manual in one place was read nowhere else, so the pre-flight gate reported the configuration OK and the publish failed on it anyway. The gate now verifies something actually honours each declaration. Open issues are checked before a tag too -- each must be fixed or carry a written reason it waits, and a reason naming an older release does not carry forward

Networking: a server that wrote a response and then closed the socket could lose the whole response on Windows loopback. The reader got a connection reset and zero bytes rather than a short read, even though every byte had been accepted and had arrived. TCPSocket and TCPSecureSocket gain CloseGracefully(), which reads until the peer hangs up and then closes, so the client owns the teardown -- not being the side that closes first is the entire remedy. Measured over 180 transfers of a 16KB response: Close() lost 21 of them, CloseGracefully() lost none. It is bounded on both sides and cannot park a thread, giving up after a second of silence or 16 reads of a peer that keeps sending instead of closing. The platform behaviour itself is not addressable from the sending side -- seven candidate socket-level fixes were measured and none of them worked, which is why the remedy is about who closes rather than about any socket option

Language server: concurrent analysis was correct only because it was serialized behind one global lock, so every editor request queued behind every other one. Underneath it, TreeFactory and TypeFactory were process-wide singletons sharing ScopeTable cursors, and the lock was compensating for that rather than fixing it. The factories are now bound per thread through an RAII scope guard, so each analysis gets its own and the thousands of existing call sites need no change, and the coarse lock gives way to per-program locking. Concurrent analysis also became a gating regression test, having previously been something run by hand

Release pipeline: four publish steps had been reporting completed/success while doing nothing. Upload to Sourceforge uploaded nothing, Publish VS Code Extension published nothing, Deploy playground deployed nothing, and Deploy API Documentation deployed nothing -- each skipped on an absent credential and passed. None of those secrets has ever been set, so those steps had likely never once run, and v2026.8.4 published with all four green: the playground was left serving a three-month-old engine and objeck.org a release-old set of API docs, including 404s on the 39 Game.OpenGL pages that were that release's headline feature. Both were repaired by hand after publishing. A missing credential is now a failure that names the secret, or a step declared manual in one place that also prints as a to-do; either way the release report matches what happened

Release pipeline: a pre-flight gate for whether the pipeline can perform the steps it advertises. Every existing gate checked the repository -- version consistency, tag state, docs, api.zip -- and none checked configuration, so the cheapest place to learn a step cannot run was during the release, after the tag was pushed. check_release_config.sh cross-references every secret the release workflows reference against what is actually set and against the declared-manual list, and fails before the tag with the command to fix or declare each gap

Release pipeline: the VS Code extension publish job has been removed rather than fixed. There is no publisher account and a gallery query for the extension id returns nothing, so it was scaffolding for a channel that was never set up -- v2026.8.4 recorded a successful publish that has never happened. The extension itself still builds and still ships as objeck-lsp_<VERSION>.zip attached to the release, installed with the scripts the client README already documents, so no advertised capability disappears

Release pipeline: the API-docs deploy now verifies the site rather than the copy. rsync exiting 0 is not objeck.org serving the new pages, so the job fetches the published reference and fails unless its version stamp matches the release -- the same correction already applied to the playground deploy, which runs code instead of reading its own health constant

Game.OpenGL: a 3D framework -- OpenGL 3.3 core over SDL2, on Windows, Linux and macOS. 26 classes covering windowing and frame pacing, built-in shaders, meshes and OBJ loading, textures, matrices and cameras, materials, up to eight directional/point/spot lights with Blinn-Phong specular, shadow maps including omnidirectional cube shadows, render-to-texture, instancing through a one-call PropBatch, frustum culling, raycasting for hitscan and picking, gamepad input, a pixel-space text overlay, and a scene that answers collision. The examples got SHORTER as it grew -- the minimal window demo went from 105 lines to 25, and per-frame allocations in both original draw loops went to zero. Verified by 453 checks that each read pixels back rather than merely exiting cleanly. 3d_gl_24.obs and fps_gl.obs -- a first-person shooting gallery with hitscan shooting, sliding collision and a controller -- both ship in the distribution

Windows: SDL2's DLLs shipped in lib/sdl, but Windows resolves a dynamically-loaded library's imports against the executable's directory -- never the directory holding the library -- so libobjk_sdl.dll failed to load for anyone who had not put lib/sdl on PATH themselves. Every SDL program was affected, 2D and 3D alike, and the regression runner hid it by prepending the directory before running the tests. The DLLs now ship in bin beside the tools that load them, which is where every other native library's dependencies already were

Documentation: the API reference and the editor index were both missing whole bundles, for two reasons. Five files hard-code the library list and had drifted apart -- one was short two libraries and still named a third that had been deleted, so the counts matched and nothing looked wrong; a CI check now set-diffs all five against the sources. Underneath that, the doc parser was reading prose as code: the word 'bundle' in a comment (and inside a string literal holding an example) re-pointed every class after it to a bundle named after the next word, and a '#' comment inside a consts block or an '@' in a class comment made the whole block unparseable. Game.SDL2 had ONE of its 41 classes correctly filed. The API reference gained 33 pages and the editor index 22 classes

Updater: 'obu update' and 'obu rollback' now work on Windows. The in-place swap needed no copy-self-and-re-exec dance after all -- Windows forbids DELETING a running executable but permits RENAMING one, and the swap already moved the current tree aside rather than deleting it, so the running obu.exe travels into .previous and keeps executing. Verified by a test that installs obu into the very tree it then replaces. Not yet covered: an MSI-installed tree keeps its old Add/Remove Programs entry, since reconciling the installer's registry entries is not implemented, and elevation against a real Program Files install is untested

Security: obu built a shell command line to fetch release metadata, so a URL carrying shell metacharacters was a command-injection vector (CWE-78, reported as a critical CodeQL finding). The tag allowlist meant the '--channel' route was not exploitable, but the guard sat far from the sink and said nothing about URLs read out of a release's own JSON. curl now runs through an argument vector on every platform and no shell is involved anywhere in obu

Updater: 'obu check' had no offline test coverage on ANY platform -- it built its own request URL instead of going through the one function that honors the offline test hook, so it always hit the live network. On Windows, where 'check' is the only supported command, that left the test hooks with nothing to attach to at all. Both commands now share one path, the release-tag guard runs before the hook rather than after it, and the updater's offline suite runs on Windows as well as Linux

Documentation: the API reference shipped inside v2026.8.1 and v2026.8.2 was v2026.8.0's. The packaging step added into the existing tracked archive instead of replacing it, so on the runs where doc generation emitted nothing the previous release's 439 pages survived untouched -- and every structural check passed against those stale entries, reporting success. The archive is now deleted before it is rebuilt, and the packaged pages are verified against the version they were generated for rather than merely counted

Release notes: the Downloads table in every drafted release body offered a macOS Intel (x64) build that is not produced and never has been -- the build matrix has a single macOS leg. It also named .tar.gz archives where the published files are .tgz, so the extract command printed directly beneath the table matched no shipped file, omitted the MSI and PKG installers most users want, and wrapped every entry in an empty link that rendered as a link and went nowhere. The table now lists the real published set and points at the Assets section

Documentation: the README's Quick Start install block still downloaded the previous release -- the first command a new user copies, silently installing the wrong version. The standing claim that all Windows installers are digitally signed has been replaced with what is checkable: it sat in the README unchanged through the four months in which every Windows MSI shipped unsigned

Release tooling: release monitoring and the post-publish steps are now two tested scripts rather than prose instructions, and the checks that guard a release fail when a verification step did not run instead of when a job merely reports green

Web.Server: the bundle shipped in every release and could not be used by anyone. Its 13 native entry points appeared in exactly one file -- the binding itself -- with no .cpp, no build target and no library in any deploy tree; nothing set the property that names the library, and Request and Response declared no constructor, so a program could not obtain an instance at all. Writing the missing native library was never available as a fix: the design is a per-host bridge whose doc comment names Nginx, IIS and Apache, whose request structures are entirely different, so a single generic library is not a thing that can exist. It is now implemented in pure Objeck over Web.HTTP.Server, which already provided a complete tested Request/Response -- same bundle, same class names, same method signatures, no native library and no new build target. Coverage went from 0 of 13 methods to 13 of 13

Networking: a server that wrote a response and immediately closed it could lose the data on Windows loopback -- measured at roughly 47% of responses -- because the sender tearing down first discards what the receiver has not yet read. HTTP now uses keep-alive, which removes the exposure rather than papering over it by changing which side closes. Alongside it: a short send() silently dropped the remainder of the buffer on BOTH platforms, a real HTTP 500 lost its body while a dead socket reported one, discarded queued response data was not closed, closed sockets read as open, and persistence framing disagreed between HTTP and HTTPS

Winsock: one failed name lookup shut down Winsock for the whole process. WSAStartup runs once, so the WSACleanup on that error path dropped the refcount to zero and closed every open socket on every thread, over a single failed lookup on a single connection. Dormant in practice only because getaddrinfo on a literal address does not fail

JIT: 64-bit immediates were truncated to 32 bits -- on AMD64 for and, or, xor, add and sub, and on Windows ARM64 for every one of them, where 'long' is 32 bits under LLP64. This is the worst class of bug the compiler can have: no crash and no diagnostic, just arithmetic that silently produced the wrong answer above 2^31. A stored float compare also clobbered a callee-saved register on AMD64. Windows ARM64 had shipped untested since February, which is why its variant survived

Garbage collector: three ways a live object could be collected or corrupted at the native boundary. An array returned by a VM trap held elements a minor collection could destroy -- measured at 395 of 395 entries lost on one collection, since arrays are born old, objects are born young, and the trap array was never dirtied through the write barrier. A value returned by a native library could be collected out of a reused argument buffer. And the JIT's Int[] copy dropped the write barrier entirely

Windows ARM64: the distribution shipped without the runtimes it needs -- no C++ redistributable, because VCToolsRedistDir is empty on the ARM64 runner, and OpenCV without its image codecs. Nothing checked, so both produced installs that failed on the user's machine rather than in CI. Cross-architecture native dependencies are now verified during the build

Virtual machine: a program that started a server and then returned normally from Main segfaulted during teardown on Windows, losing every line of buffered output with it -- so it looked like the program had done nothing when it had in fact run to completion. A thread blocked in a syscall never observes the halt request, so teardown freed the program image while that thread was still live; the WSACleanup on the way out then unblocked it and sent it executing against freed memory. Linux was always clean for exactly one reason: it has no equivalent call. The program image is no longer freed while a thread may still run against it

Debugger: obd had the same teardown defect as the VM, and there it was NOT Windows-only. obd hosts the debuggee's VM in-process, and its ClearProgram ran after every single run -- freeing the bytecode image, the program, and the whole GC heap, since clearing the heap releases the young region, every old-generation object and the locks the VM takes on the way in. It halted and waited for nothing at all. Because obd outlives the run and goes back to its prompt, an ordinary client connecting to the port the parked thread sits on wakes it with no WSACleanup involved -- 6 access violations in 6 runs on Windows and 2 in 2 on Linux, beside 8 in 8 for the DAP session-exit shape, which was Windows-only. Debugging a server program is now something you can do without the debugger dying on the way out

Debugger: obd could not debug ANY multithreaded program. Compile one with -debug -- which is how you compile a program you intend to debug -- and obd segfaulted on the first instruction the spawned thread executed, before that thread printed a line. The interpreter's debugger pointer was set by exactly one constructor, and spawned VM threads use a different one, which left it holding garbage while the per-instruction hook called through it. It looked like a -debug problem rather than a threading one because the hook touches nothing until a line number exists, and without debug symbols every line number is -1. Only obd is built with the hook compiled in, so obr was never affected and the VM regression suite could not have caught it. Breakpoints and stepping still do not reach inside spawned threads, but the threads run

macOS: notarization had been failing on every release, silently, and the ONNX binding aborted the process when destroying its environment at exit. Releases now ship as a notarizable .zip and the failure is no longer swallowed

Performance: native calls got materially cheaper. A string literal allocates on every evaluation, and the literal naming the native function was 92% of a call's cost -- 1655ns down to 130ns. Resolved entry points are now cached as well, on every platform: every call had been converting the name from wide to narrow and asking the loader for its address (GetProcAddress walks a DLL's export table, dlsym walks the module's symbol hash) for a name that never changes, at 110ns per call. Both are guarded by CI so neither can drift back

Debugger: one malformed DAP request could end the whole session. Only JSON parse errors were guarded, so a message that parsed but carried an unexpected type threw from inside the handler, unwound out of Run() to a main() with no handler, and terminated the process -- losing every breakpoint and the running program over a single bad request. Dispatch now answers with a DAP error response instead

Debugger: seven flags shared between the DAP thread and the VM thread were written under a mutex but read without one, at every instruction. Beyond torn reads, nothing stopped an -O3 -flto build hoisting those loads out of the dispatch loop, so a disconnect or step request could go unseen indefinitely. All seven are atomics now

Debugger: an undecodable console line silently re-ran the PREVIOUS command. ReadLine appended rather than assigned and left the prior contents in place when decoding failed, so the stale buffer was handed back and executed again

Network: a connect that never completed could be reported as successful, and both the POSIX and Windows connect-with-timeout paths could hand back a socket still in non-blocking mode -- a caller expecting a blocking read got a spurious EAGAIN/WSAEWOULDBLOCK instead of data. The unchecked F_GETFL behind the POSIX case also restored garbage flags onto the socket

REPL: the full-screen editor could hang instead of returning an error, stalling inside read() on a child process that had not written yet; the failure path now also reaps the child rather than leaving a zombie writing into a closed pipe

REPL: a garbled terminal escape sequence could store bytes outside the ECMA-48 parameter ranges as negative characters before being fed to atoi; malformed sequences are now rejected the same way a short read already was

Compiler: a corrupt or crafted .obl could crash the compiler. TypeParser::ParseType and ParseParameters switch on the first character of a type string and had no default case, so anything outside the known set -- including an EMPTY string, whose operator[](0) yields a null character -- left the type null and was dereferenced immediately. The linker calls both on type strings read straight out of library files, so the input is not the compiler's own

Compiler: a lambda whose signature collided with an existing method was silently dropped. AddMethod returns false on a collision and the result was ignored, so the code carried on encoding and associating a method that had never been registered, with no diagnostic at all. A separate case left MethodCall's func_ref_unwrap indeterminate in one of its five constructors, and the emitter tests that pointer before emitting through it -- so non-null garbage meant emitting a bogus call

REPL: a buffer whose first non-empty line is '}' hung the REPL, on listing and on save. An unsigned indent counter was decremented at 0, wrapping to SIZE_MAX, and the indent loop below then ran about 1.8e19 times

Runtime: every float written to stderr came out in whatever format the last call happened to set. StdErrFloat read the saved stream state from std::wcout, modified std::wcerr and restored onto std::cout -- three different objects -- so wcerr kept the fixed/scientific/precision setting permanently while narrow std::cout had its flags overwritten

ONNX: a single SLM or vision call left every float an Objeck program printed for the rest of the run in fixed notation at one decimal. Both generation reports applied std::fixed with setprecision(1) directly to std::wcout and never restored it, and nothing on the Objeck side could clear a leaked floatfield. They now format through a local stream, so wcout's state is never touched

Tooling: obc, obr, obd and obi each had a long unprotected prologue -- locale and codecvt construction, and the usage-string building that is a bad_alloc path -- so anything thrown there called terminate() with no message. Every entry point is now wrapped. In the multithreaded collector, a free-list size counter mutated under one lock and read without it became an atomic, and the sweep/mark lock hierarchy is recorded at both lock sites

Language: subscript the result of a method call -- 'GetItems()[0]->GetName()' now works. It had never been implemented and the grammar swallowed the attempt, so 'GetArr()[0]->Size()' silently returned 1. Behaviour change: code that compiled and returned the wrong value now returns the correct one
Release: the release build now compiles and runs a real program from the shipped tree and asserts its version matches the tag; every earlier gate only checked that files existed

ONNX: face detection never returned a single face -- FaceSession->Detect and ->Recognize produced zero results for every image at every threshold, on every platform shipping the ONNX native library, since v2026.5.3, while inference itself ran normally. scrfd_decode compared a row count against an element count, so every stride group was skipped. Verified with the InsightFace buffalo_l models: 2 faces in the sample group photo, 512-dimensional embeddings, same-person similarity 0.767 and different-person -0.023. YOLO and ResNet were unaffected

Packaging: obu was missing from every v2026.8.0 archive. The release advertised the updater as a headline feature and delivered no binary -- the build never referenced obu and none of the three deploy scripts copied it, so bin/ held obb, obc, obd, obi and obr on every platform. CI missed it because the updater's own test builds a separate copy with test hooks, so obu was tested continuously while never being shipped. It is now installed to bin/ by all three deploy scripts, and both binary-verification gates list it

Documentation: Web.HTTP.HeaderCheck shipped with only IsValidRequestTarget documented. IsValidName and IsValidValue -- the validators behind every AddHeader call -- had no doc comment, and the API index records only documented members, so hover and completion showed nothing for them. Flatten's doc block was also attached to the wrong function. All four are now documented

Editor: obi gains a full-screen editor ('/e') — raw-mode terminal editing over the REPL buffer with syntax coloring from the compiler's own scanner, damage-diffed rendering, CJK/tab-correct widths, undo/redo, Shift-selection and an opt-in vi profile; F5 compiles and runs the buffer as a cancellable subprocess and F8 walks the cursor through compile errors

Network: HTTP/3 now works on Windows 11 / Server 2022 and later over WinHTTP/MsQuic — it had shipped documented-and-dead, with the API present and every request failing; requests assert the protocol actually used rather than silently downgrading

Security: five HTTP request-injection fixes — a CR/LF in a URL path could split the request line itself, and caller-supplied header values and content types were injectable across HTTP/1.1, HTTPS, HTTP/2 and HTTP/3; HTTP/3 connection IDs could also be uninitialised stack memory when the CSPRNG failed

Tooling: the obu updater — 'obu check' compares against the latest release, and 'obu update'/'obu rollback' (Linux/macOS) verify a SHA-256 digest before touching disk, then stage an all-or-nothing swap with automatic rollback
JIT: the ARM64 backend clobbered a general register on every float compare against memory, and zeroed the divisor of every JIT float division — the long-open "memory corruption of free block" crash

Compiler: 'v->Pow(10)' computed Pow(10, v) whenever the receiver was a variable, instance variable or array element, affecting all 29 multi-argument primitive functions; divide and modulus by zero now trap cleanly at every optimization level

Language: nil-safe operators — 'a?->b()' calls b only when a is non-Nil and yields Nil instead of faulting, and 'a ?? b' supplies b when a is Nil; a single '?->' guards the whole rest of a chain, and both desugar onto the existing Try()/Otherwise() intrinsics so no new bytecode is emitted

Language server: fixed five requests that crashed the server outright — go-to-implementation, semantic tokens, inlay hints, and both call-hierarchy directions — plus a line-range bug that made any cursor past the first method of a class resolve to the first method, affecting definition, references, hover and rename
Formatter: '??' is no longer split into '? ?', which had produced source that would not compile
Tooling: the formatter, language server and VS Code extension are now covered by CI

VM: fixed an intermittent multithreaded crash in the generational minor garbage collector — a thread being spawned held its self/param as untracked pointers, so a moving collection during the spawn handoff could leave the new thread a stale reference; these are now tracked and relocated across collection

VM: generational minor garbage collection is now enabled — nursery-full collections scan only the remembered set plus roots and recycle the nursery without sweeping old gen, with a major-GC fallback under old-gen pressure; JIT and interpreter reference stores emit the write barrier on AMD64 and ARM64

Language: closure ergonomics — call a FuncRef directly with v(), bare lambdas with an inferred return type (\() => x) that auto-wrap into FuncRef<R> in assignments, returns, method arguments, and collection elements, and lambda block bodies
Fixes: multi-capture closure heap corruption (closure-local capture ids); ARM64 negative-offset JIT load/stores (signed LDUR/STUR)
Documentation: API reference code examples now render as formatted, syntax-highlighted blocks — the ONNX library examples previously appeared as run-on inline text
Tooling: the release-process skills (version bump, release, docs, playground deploy) are now versioned in the repo
Language: string interpolation with expressions and format specifiers ("{$pi:.2}", "{$total * rate}") plus String->Format positional templating
Language: generics with bounds, F-bounds, and declaration-site variance (out/in covariance/contravariance)
VM: cooperative multithreaded stop-the-world garbage collection with JIT safepoints on AMD64 and ARM64

Debugger: major command-line (obd) and VS Code (DAP) upgrade — frame navigation, locals, set-variable, method/conditional/temporary breakpoints, watchpoints, function breakpoints, logpoints, in-process restart, and exception breakpoints
Security: TLS and DTLS clients verify server certificates by default; hardened untrusted-input deserialization
Libraries: new Web.Server HTTP library; reproducible byte-identical .obl builds
Fixes: serialization correctness (64-bit ints and Int[], function-reference fields); compiler LICM/ConstantProp; macOS ONNX CoreML cache (~35x faster warm starts)
Compiler: Tail Call Optimization (TCO) — self-recursive tail calls rewritten to jumps, eliminating stack growth (-opt s1+)
Compiler: Loop-Invariant Code Motion (LICM) — hoists arr->Size() reads and pure arithmetic out of loop bodies (-opt s2+)
VM: Auto-JIT now compiles methods containing MTHD_CALL after 10 invocations (5-15% speedup across benchmarks)
VM: Extended interpreter fast-path with 15 additional inline opcodes (comparisons, bitwise, shifts, logical)
Performance: bench_matrix_multiply -14%, bench_dead_code -15%, bench_array_intensive -12%, binarytrees -7%, mandelbrot -6%
Fixed bugs #501 and #503
Added library support for JSON-RPC
Code generation optimized to eliminate redundant labels
Added trim front and back to the 'System.String'
Refactored the 'Collections.Stack' class to be list vs. array based
Fixed bugs #501 and #502
Support for strings in select statement
Bug fixes
Fixed REPL start up issues
Code refactoring for performance
